# How to Patiently Walk an Older Parent Through a New Phone App

> **In short:** A six-step method for teaching an older parent one small app task at their own pace — using *their* words for each button, writing the steps on paper so they can refer back without you, and finishing with a moment of independence that builds real confidence.

When you finally sit down with a parent to show them a new app, the goal isn't really that they get it today. The goal is that they feel capable enough to try it again tomorrow — without calling you for every little thing. This guide is a slow, kind way to teach that sticks.

## Before you start
- The phone or tablet your parent will use, charged and unlocked.
- The app they're learning is already installed (or you install it together in the first few minutes).
- A pen and a piece of paper — yes, real paper, on purpose.
- About 30 minutes of unhurried time where neither of you has to rush off.

## Step 1 — Pick one small goal, not the whole app
Decide on **one** thing they should be able to do by the end of the session. *"Send me a photo"* is a great goal. *"Learn WhatsApp"* is too big. A small goal gives them a clear finish line, and finishing feels good. Say it out loud: *"Today we're just going to learn how to send me a photo. That's it."* If they want to keep going after that, fine — but the goal is set and small.

💬 Example goal: *"By the end of today, you'll be able to send me one photo using the camera button."*

You'll know it worked when they can name the one thing they learned in plain words.

## Step 2 — Sit beside them, not across from them
Sit on the same side of the table, or next to them on the couch, so you're both looking at the screen the same way. **Hand them the phone — don't hold it yourself.** When you hold it, you're driving. They need to feel the buttons under their own thumb. Reach over only to point, never to grab. If you feel the urge to take the phone and *"just show them quickly,"* that urge is the thing to fight.

If the room is bright or the screen looks washed out, tilt the phone so the glare goes away. If they wear reading glasses, make sure they're on before any tiny text appears.

You'll know it worked when their finger is the one tapping the screen, not yours.

## Step 3 — Ask them to try first, then watch what they do
Before you explain anything, hand them the phone and say: *"Show me how you'd try to send me a photo."* Don't correct them while they try — just watch. You'll learn two things: what they already understand, and which part trips them up. That trip-up point is exactly where your teaching needs to begin. It's often not where you expected.

If they freeze and say *"I don't know,"* that's fine. Reply: *"That's why I'm here — try anyway, even if it's wrong."* Pressing the wrong button is how they learn which button is right.

💬 Example prompt to them: *"Just tap anywhere you think might help. There's no wrong move yet."*

You'll know it worked when you can name the one spot they got stuck.

## Step 4 — Walk through one tap at a time, in their words
Now teach — but only one tap at a time. Hold their finger (gently) if needed, point at the screen, and say each thing out loud in plain language. **Use their words for the buttons, not the app's official names.** If they call the camera icon *"the little camera picture,"* write that down. If they call the send button *"the blue paper airplane,"* that's what it is now. The point isn't to teach them the app's vocabulary — it's to teach them a route they can remember.

Say things like *"Now tap the blue paper airplane"* instead of *"Now tap the send button."* Repeat the same words every time you refer to the same thing — consistency is what makes it stick.

You'll know it worked when they start whispering your words to themselves before tapping.

## Step 5 — Write each step on paper, in their words
While they watch (or while they tap it themselves once more), grab the pen and paper. Write the steps as **numbered, plain sentences** — short, no jargon, using the words *they* just used. For example: *"1. Tap the little camera picture. 2. Tap the big blue circle to take the photo. 3. Tap the blue paper airplane to send."* Hand them the paper. Tell them they can stick it on the fridge or keep it next to the phone charger.

**Don't take a screenshot.** Screenshots are tiny, full of unfamiliar icons, and live inside the very phone they can't navigate. Paper lives where they can see it and ask someone else to read it if they forget.

If their handwriting is shaky or they don't want to write, you write it for them in big, neat letters.

You'll know it worked when the paper is in their hand, not yours.

## Step 6 — Let them do it alone, then book a check-in
Now the hardest part: sit back, fold your arms, and let them do the whole thing again from step 1, alone. No hints unless they're truly stuck. If they forget a step, point at the paper on the table — don't tap the screen for them. Watch them succeed. Celebrate specifically: *"You found the paper airplane all by yourself."* Before you leave, say: *"Try doing this twice more before I visit again. If you get stuck, write your question down and we'll go through it next time."*

If they can't quite finish alone today, that's okay. Shorten the paper list to two steps, or schedule another short session next week. Confidence grows in small sittings, not long marathons.

You'll know it worked when they can do it start-to-finish while you just sit and watch.

## Common mistakes
- **Rushing to "just show them" by taking the phone.** The fix: keep the phone in their hand at all times. Your job is to point, not to drive.
- **Using the app's official button names instead of theirs.** The fix: write down whatever they call each thing, even if it's *"the little yellow bell"* — that's their word, and that's the one that works.
- **Skipping the paper because "screenshots are easier."** The fix: paper beats screenshots for tired eyes, lives outside the phone, and doubles as a fridge-door reminder that you believe they can do this.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** This same slow method works the next time you teach them anything new — a TV remote, a microwave, a new password, a new key fob.
- **For your family:** The paper cheat sheet lives on the fridge, and you stop getting *"how do I…"* phone calls at 9 p.m. — which means more evening time for both of you.
- **If you're just starting with this approach:** Pick the smallest possible goal for the first session. Confidence builds faster than knowledge does, and one small win makes the next lesson easier.

## Try it now
Pick one small app action your parent has been wanting to learn, then write down the three steps it would take — using only words *they* would use. Bring that piece of paper to your next visit.
